1.pericope_label: The sons' murmuring, Laban's countenance, and the command to return

schools.summary: Calvin turns first on Jacob: his patience appears in suspending his purpose until a new occasion offered, yet imperfection was mixed with it, since for the sake of wealth he put off his return six years when Laban's changing of terms would have justified bidding him farewell, the tardiness being probably connected with indolence. Had Laban treated him kindly his mind would have been lulled asleep; he is driven off instead by adverse looks, for God often secures his people's salvation better by subjecting them to the hatred of the wicked than by letting them be soothed with bland address. On the sons he is harder: avaricious men think themselves robbed of whatever they have not gorged themselves with, and never ask whether the wealth was got justly. The two generations betray it differently — the young men give their vexation vent, while the father, like a cunning old fox, says nothing and lets his face speak. On the command he sees the timidity plainly, since Jacob, perceiving what was designed against him, still dared not move a foot without a new oracle: adversity may incite us to duty, but we profit little unless the word is added. Gill supposes Jacob heard the words in their tents or in the field, or from wives and friends who thought fit to tell him.

Henry, whom Wesley abridges, thinks the words spoken in Jacob's hearing on purpose to vex him, and sets the scene against the chapter before: that one opened with Rachel envying Leah, this one with Laban's sons envying Jacob. He weighs their two charges. They magnify the prosperity — all this glory — and what was it? a parcel of brown sheep and speckled goats, some camels and asses; riches are glorious things in carnal eyes, and the overvaluing of worldly wealth is the root from which covetousness and envy grow. Then they impeach his honesty, that he has taken all that was their father's — not all, surely, for what had become of the cattle committed to their own keeping and sent three days' journey off? He turns the countenance to use as well: Laban was a churl at best and now more churlish, envy being a sin that shows in the face, and sour looks doing much toward the ruin of peace in a family, so that Laban's angry face justly lost him the greatest blessing his house ever had. Against that he sets the command, that Jacob had met hard usage but would not quit his place till God bade him, having come by orders from heaven.

Clarke finds the jealousy natural, the multiplication of Jacob's cattle and the decline of Laban's being visible to anyone, and observes that the word for glory means both to be rich and to be heavy — perhaps because riches always bring a heavy burden of cares. On the promise he reads a pledge of the same care on the return as on the way out, and notes the Targum's rendering that God's Word should be his help.

Ellicott doubts the arithmetic: no sons of Laban have been mentioned before, and if by the same wife as Leah and Rachel they would now be men of fifty-five or sixty; their claim was exaggeration, since Laban was still rich and had probably gained on the whole by so gifted a man's presence, and their word glory shows Jacob had become a person of consequence among the people of Haran. He identifies the revelation with the dream described further on, ascribed there to Elohim and here to Jehovah, the narrator meaning to show that the providence Jacob took for the work of Elohim was really the guardianship of the covenant God. Keil pauses on a pronoun, the fuller form here standing behind the abbreviation found later.

4.pericope_label: Jacob's case laid before his wives: the changed wages and the dream

schools.summary: Calvin makes the division two, integrity against perfidy and then the prosperity ascribed to God, meant to make Rachel and Leah the readier to go; having grown rich in a short space, Jacob clears himself by appealing to them as witnesses of the diligence they had watched for twenty years. He dwells on the risk: it was difficult to carry women who had never left their father's house into a remote country by an unknown road, and there was ground to fear they might betray their husband in seeking their own protection, so Jacob showed constancy in exposing himself rather than failing in a husband's duty — and God gave him more than he asked, the wives whose strifes had once filled the house freely agreeing to go into exile. Of the angel in the dream he thinks it no wonder that he should assume the person of God, either because the Father appeared to the patriarchs in his own Word under an angel's form, or because angels speaking at God's command utter their words as from his mouth; and God calls himself the God of Bethel not as confined to a place but to renew the remembrance of his promise. Gill argues this was no created angel but the eternal one, the Son of God, afterwards called God, and one to whom Jacob vowed a vow, which he would never have done to an angel; he also fills out what the wives had witnessed — faithfulness and uprightness, industry and prudence, the best methods contrived and no pains spared by day or night.

Clarke explains why the wives were fetched to the flocks rather than visited in their tents: he was at some distance with the sheep, and in the tents Laban's household might overhear, though Laban himself was three days' journey off. On the ten times he reports a strange diversity — Aquila has ten numbers, Symmachus ten times in number, the Septuagint ten lambs, which Origen seems to follow, and one authority takes the ten lambs for five years' wages — but thinks it most natural to read the phrase as indefinite, meaning frequently, and lists the parallels of ten women baking in one oven and the ten times of reproach. He finds it strange that no such dream has been reported before, and notes that the Samaritan gives it whole at the end of the previous chapter; on the colour word he derives grisled from the French for hail, white spots upon a dark ground. Wesley says only that Jacob wished to talk with them more privately.

Ellicott notes Rachel put first as the chief wife, and that in open pasture the three ran no risk of being overheard. He divides the speech into three — the change in Laban's manner and the fear it bred, the defence of his conduct with a charge of repeated injustice, and the announcement of the command to return — and on the middle part concedes what the wives must have known, that Jacob had used stratagems to increase his wages; but Laban had openly broken the bargain, for when the parti-coloured young multiplied beyond expectation he first allowed only the speckled, the commonest, and at last only the ringstraked, the rarest. He dismisses the ten times in four words, a good many times, and corrects two others: the rams are properly he-goats, and grisled means spotted as with hailstones. Keil makes ten a round number for completeness, and infers the history behind it, that seeing so many mottled young born to sheep of one colour Laban kept trying to narrow the original stipulation; he adds that Jacob says nothing here of his own stratagem, representing the whole increase as the fruit of God's blessing.

14.pericope_label: The wives' answer, the flight, and the stolen images

schools.summary: Calvin finds the answer a case of all things working together for good: women unjustly used by their father act against the natural tenderness of their sex and consent to follow a husband into an unknown country, so that Jacob, who had swallowed many bitter draughts, is repaid by not losing his wives to their attachment to their father's house. Their argument he states plainly — daughters cling to a father because reckoned members of his family, but this one passed them off without dowry, set them to sale, and devoured the price. Yet he will not let the reasoning stand: they confirm their husband's speech in a common rather than a religious spirit, resting the weight on a slighter argument, that what they carried off was their own unpaid inheritance, never that the wealth was justly earned by their husband's labour, so that they obscure the blessing of God and undervalue his toil by boasting that its fruit came of themselves — here is no precedent for recovering a right unjustly wrested from us. He marks the constancy of the going: the moment his wives consented Jacob yielded to no further obstacle, though Moses leaves the reader to supply what lay between. Gill says Laban had treated them neither as children nor as freeborn persons, but as foreigners taken in war or bought of others, or as bondmaids born in his house whom he might sell; and he records the Jewish reckoning of the flocks at five thousand five hundred.

Henry defends the manner of the going three times over. It was lawful to leave such service without warning, warranted by God's express order and by the law of self-preservation; prudent to steal away unawares, lest Laban hinder or plunder him; and honest to carry off no more than his own, taking what Providence had given and not undertaking to repair his own damages. On the images he allows that Rachel was not so honest as her husband, and canvasses what the teraphim were: some take them for small representations of the family's ancestors, statues or pictures she wished to carry into another country, but it should rather seem they were images for religious use, household gods worshipped or consulted as oracles. He hopes with bishop Patrick that she took them neither for the metal nor for her own use, but to convince her father how foolish it was to regard as gods what could not secure themselves.

Clarke thinks they gave their father his true character: he used them as slaves he might dispose of, sold them for gain, applied the price to his own use, and allowed them neither portion nor inheritance. Wesley takes both claims without weighing them — Jacob called the wealth his wages and they their portions, and either way God forced Laban to pay his debts, to servant and daughters alike.

Ellicott hears the asperity and draws an inference: not only the petted Rachel but the neglected Leah joins in, and though the open sale and the withheld portion were old sores long since healed, Laban must have been grasping of late to keep their memory so fresh in his daughters. Keil describes the teraphim as small images in human form worshipped as givers of prosperity and consulted for answers, and on Jacob's going explains the idiom, that to steal a man's heart is to take away his knowledge of a thing, and so deceive him.

19.pericope_label: Rachel's theft, the stolen heart, and the crossing to Gilead

schools.summary: Calvin will not have the theft excused. The word is commonly used in a bad sense and Laban himself soon calls them his gods, so the propensity of the mind to idolatry stands exposed: not two hundred years from Noah's death, with Shem's teaching still sounding in their ears, the filth of superstition had flooded the very family God had chosen as his one sanctuary on earth, and Jacob had spent twenty years admonishing them in vain. That Rachel was not healed in all that time he finds more absurd still: she was so wedded to what she had imbibed from childhood that she was ready to infect the chosen land, imagining she followed God while carrying off the idols that would subvert his worship. To those who excuse her as purging her father's house by a pious theft he puts two questions — why then did she not throw the abominations into the Euphrates as she crossed, and why did she never tell her husband? The sequel settles it, the house of Jacob being polluted with idols down to the violation of Dinah. On the departure he shows the straits Jacob was in, having no hope but flight, since Laban had meant to hold him for life like a slave bound to the soil. Gill thinks Jacob too cunning for the Syrian, whose astrology gave no foresight of the flight, and asks whether the stolen heart means Laban's knowledge or the cattle he coveted, preferring the first.

What the teraphim were Clarke calls utterly unknown, and lays out the guesses. They are called Laban's gods later, and some take them for images used superstitiously without being reckoned gods, representatives rather of divine attributes; Theodoret calls them idols outright and holds that Rachel, a type of the true Church, stole them to deliver her father from idolatry, which is nearly Jarchi's reason. The Targum of Jonathan gives the strangest turn, that a first-born man had been murdered and his head embalmed with spices, divinations written on a plate of gold and laid under his tongue, and the thing set against a wall, where it conversed with them and Laban worshipped it. Clarke's own guess derives the word from a root meaning to heal, which would make them talismans against disease, kept as the Romans kept their household gods. He also raises a difficulty nobody else feels, how the flocks were got over the Euphrates: the rabbins claim a miracle and a dry crossing, and since we know no other way it is prudent to refer it to God's power, though fords may have been known. Wesley notes that the flock being sheared was the part in his sons' hands, three days off.

Ellicott fills out the occasion: shearing was a joyous time, the shearers' toil relieved with feasting, and the household would have been busy at it. He observes that Laban's wealth was not diminished, only no longer increasing, then asks why Jacob, who had chief charge of the flocks, was not there — possibly he was expected and missed, more probably, as the estrangement grew with the increase of his riches, Laban and his sons had taken the management back into their own hands. He follows the teraphim through the later history: Michal laid them in David's bed, from which he gathers a head shaped like a man's but a stunted trunk, while the pair Rachel hid under the camel's furniture must have been small; and since Nebuchadnezzar divines by them he thinks them possibly Chaldean, less worshipped than consulted, and supposes Rachel took them expecting prosperity for her husband and herself. On the flight he explains that the heart was the seat of the intellect, so to steal it is to elude a man's observation. Keil sets the clock running: Laban was not told for three days, and pursued seven more before overtaking.

22.pericope_label: The pursuit, the warning in the dream, and Laban's first charges

schools.summary: Gill accounts for the three days' delay by the distance of the shearing from Jacob's flocks, so that Laban could not have heard sooner; he takes the brethren for kinsmen, descendants of his father's brothers, most likely living in Haran, or else for neighbours he could call on. He supposes Laban reached the mount late and saw nothing of Jacob till morning, and reports the Targum's angel, whom the Jews name Michael — rightly, he says, if the uncreated Angel is meant. Calvin watches the tone rather than the matter: his cruelty bridled, Laban dared not threaten, but laid his ferocity aside for feigned blandishments and complained of injury to his paternal affection — as hypocrites do when the power of hurting is taken away, heaping false complaints on the simple as though the blame lay there.

Henry observes that God can bridle the malice of the wicked without changing their hearts, and sets out the charges as Laban framed them. First Jacob is a renegade who deserted his service, and to make that stick Laban pretends he meant nothing but kindness — he would have kissed his grandchildren, which was all he would have given them, and sent them off with mirth and songs, tabret and harp. He contrasts Rebekah's leaving the same house a hundred and twenty years before with prayers and blessings, and finds in the exchange a sign that religion had decayed there. It is common, he adds, for bad men disappointed of a malicious project to pretend they designed only what was fair; and those who mean ill put the worst construction on innocent acts, which is why the wives are said to be carried off like captives. Then Laban boasts of the power in his hand, supposing he had both right and strength — for bad men value themselves on a power to hurt, when a power to do good is worth more, and those who will do nothing to be loved are content to be feared. Yet he must own the restraint laid on him. The last charge is theft, and Henry will not let it pass: foolish man, to call those his gods which could be stolen, when enemies may take our goods but not our God.

Clarke presses the literal Hebrew, from good to evil: had Laban been forbidden to speak either good or bad they could have had no conversation at all: men meet in friendly language, and the command means, do not open with peace be unto thee and then pass to injurious words and violence. Wesley states the object bluntly, to bring Jacob back into bondage or strip him of what he had, and reads the prohibition as forbidding anything said against the journey, the thing proceeding from the Lord — observing that the safety of good men owes much to the hold God has on the consciences of bad ones.

Ellicott prefers another sense for the brethren, since Jacob later uses the word of his own followers: probably a courteous name for retainers, freemen of higher rank than servants. He works out the distances — Jacob's route was apparently the easterly one, past Tadmor and through the Hauran, and Gilead must stand for the whole region of chalk cliffs east of Jordan; even so it was three hundred miles from Haran, and would have taken hard riding. On Jacob's side he sees no difficulty: the flocks could go to the ford in detachments under the elder sons, the wives and younger children being fetched only when all was advanced — so that Jacob had reached Canaanite ground, a point of some importance, before his father-in-law came up. Keil glosses the captives phrase as sword-booty, prisoners of war taken away by force, and the parting Laban describes as a farewell feast. Ellicott calls the prohibition proverbial, carrying a more absolute prohibition than the similar phrase elsewhere.

27.pericope_label: The remaining charges, the search of the tents, and Rachel's stratagem

schools.summary: Gill hears an intimation that Laban would not have opposed the departure had he been told, so there was no need to go off like a thief; the sons he wished to kiss were grandsons, the daughters Rachel and Leah with Dinah. He cites the Jerusalem Targum's paraphrase of the boast, I have an army and a multitude; calls the oath too rashly spoken; and reports, without allowing it foundation, the Jewish claim that Rachel's death in childbirth fulfilled the imprecation. Calvin cares less for the grammar of the boast than for its contradiction: Laban had been forbidden by God, so where was the power he boasted of? He rushes on as though he could act against God's purpose, pride being always the companion of unbelief; and though compelled to yield to the God of Abraham he defrauds him of glory by keeping his fictitious deities. On Jacob's answer he marks the modesty — he excuses the secret departure as having feared to be deprived of his wives, and never disputes as a casuist whether flight by stealth was lawful. Yet on the oath Calvin turns critic: Jacob spoke from the heart, but had the truth come out he must have been ashamed of his haste, for he should have questioned wives and children instead of trusting so far to his own house's discipline — and by that haste the pollution he might have swept out at once remained longer in his family. Of Rachel he weighs shame against obstinacy and decides for obstinacy: it was the love of idolatry, not fear of her husband's sentence, that made her think anything worth attempting rather than lose so incomparable a treasure; and to the theft she added lying words.

Clarke takes the four tokens of a send-off in turn: mirth is a feast, songs are odes in praise of God or commemorating the acts of ancestors, the tabret is the tympanum still used in the east, our tambourine, and the harp a lute whose Greek name is borrowed from the Hebrew. He explains why Rachel's excuse worked: if the teraphim served any religious purpose, Laban could not suspect a woman whose touch defiled of sitting on the objects of his adoration. He also gives her a motive — she probably believed her father could learn by these very images which way they had fled, and having stolen them was afraid to own it. Wesley gives Jacob's two answers, the fear that Laban would take his daughters by force and bind him to further service, and a plain not guilty to the theft, since Jacob neither took the images nor knew of them.

Keil renders the boast literally, there is to God my hand, his hand serving him as a god — a proverbial way of saying the power lies in it; and he describes the stratagem: Laban went through every tent and missed the teraphim because Rachel had put them in her riding saddle, a seat of carpets on the packsaddle, and sat on them, pleading the custom of women. Ellicott defends the common rendering of the boast as that of all the versions, but grants Keil and Knobel's comes to the same thing impiously, making the hand an El that lets him do as he pleases. He is gentler with the man than the others, finding the speech half true and half false — Laban would rather not have parted with Jacob at all, but if he must, would have liked appearances kept up, and probably did love his daughters, though not enough to outweigh his selfishness. Of the saddle he adds that such a thing is now wicker-work under curtains and a canopy, hers probably simpler, and images with men's heads and dwarf bodies would go easily under it.

36.pericope_label: Jacob's expostulation: twenty years of service and the God of his father

schools.summary: Calvin faults Jacob for contending about a matter not sufficiently known and fastening calumny on Laban, supposing his household clear when his own negligence had deceived him; yet he resists boldly without the insolence of evil speaking, and presses his case before Laban's kinsmen so that his long patience might make his integrity plainer. He reads the departed sleep as more than wakefulness — Jacob had contended against nature so far as to defraud himself of rest. On the closing verse he takes the whole as Jacob's disclaimer: he denies that his father-in-law's kindness made him rich and ascribes it to God's favour that he goes home not empty — I owe it not to thee that thou hast not injured me further, but God withstood thee; and since God does not defend the unfaithful, Jacob's integrity appears from his standing up as vindicator. Gill grants he carried his passion too far, while judging his reasoning strong and his expostulation just.

Henry calls the outburst a lesson in the power of provocation: Jacob's temper was mild and grace had improved it, yet Laban's carriage put him into a heat, and his chiding, whatever excuse it admits, is not for our imitation, grievous words stirring up anger and making bad worse. He sets out the record point by point. Jacob was careful, so that through no neglect of his did the ewes cast their young; honest, not coveting the rams of the flock; and laborious, keeping to his work in all weathers with invincible patience — so men of business must resolve to endure hardness, and ministers, who are shepherds too, may take him for a pattern. Two kinds of bad master he finds in Laban: those who exact what is unjust, making a servant answer for damage that was no fault of his, a loss inconsiderable to the master often near ruining a poor servant; and those who deny what is just, as Laban did in making Jacob serve for his daughters and then giving them without portions. On the title Jacob uses he hears humility, and Wesley after him: he calls God the God of his father, thinking himself unworthy but beloved for his father's sake, and distinguishes the God of Abraham from the fear of Isaac because Abraham was dead and gone where perfect love casts out fear, while Isaac still lived, sanctifying the Lord in his heart as his fear and his dread.

Clarke finds in one clause the measure of Laban's rigour, since the law of God did not oblige a shepherd to make good what wild beasts had torn, and that law was likely in force from the earliest times. He names the root of the trouble, that covetousness was Laban's constitutional sin, governing his conduct and making him careless of his children's interest so long as his own was secured. But he will not leave Jacob unexamined: some earlier unfair dealing may have led him to the expedient of outwitting Laban over the parti-coloured cattle, which palliates the measure without justifying it — and almost all his conduct toward Laban is easier to excuse than the injuring of his breed by leaving him none but weak and degenerate beasts.

Ellicott sees why the anger broke out: Jacob had taken the charge about the teraphim for a pretext to search his goods, and finding nothing gave his indignation free vent. He reports the Jewish explanation of the fear of Isaac, that with his father still living Jacob would have been wanting in reverence to speak of God as Isaac's God. Keil notes that in the East the cold of night answers to the heat of day, and enters a caution of his own: the warning God gave condemned Laban's course, but did not thereby sanction what Jacob had done to increase his possessions, still less confirm that the dream was a revelation — Jacob had met cunning with cunning, and Laban had no right to punish it.

43.pericope_label: Laban's change of tone, the covenant, and the heap of witness

schools.summary: Gill notes that Laban neither denies what Jacob said nor confesses a fault, though seemingly convicted in his own conscience; and he has him perceiving that Jacob's God prospered him, and fearing that one day, grown powerful, he would avenge his usage. Calvin makes the change conscience breaking through: where had this humanity sprung from so suddenly, in a man lately bent on ruining Jacob, unless he knew Jacob had dealt faithfully? Though avarice takes away soundness of mind, a knowledge of truth remains engraven in the soul and keeps depravity from wholly triumphing. On the covenant he says Laban acts as men conscious of guilt do when they would guard against revenge, such trepidation being the just wages of evil deeds; and against that he sets Jacob's placability, since having borne many wrongs he forgets them all and stretches out his hand, so little pertinacious about his right that he anticipates Laban and is first to set up the stone — for God's children should not merely embrace peace but pursue it. On the two names he faces the difficulty that Laban used the Syrian tongue though descended from Heber — yet the two languages were so near that inflecting one into the other was easy, and Jacob, knowing his family set apart from the nations, would have made a point of teaching his own. From the double naming Calvin draws a rule, that rites must mean what those who use them agree they mean, and applies it to the sacraments: take away the word by which God covenants with us, and only useless and dead figures are left.

Henry treats the profession of kindness as a change of subject: unable to excuse what he has done, Laban owns in effect what he should have done, since he ought to have treated them as his own and had counted them strangers — those without natural affection commonly pretending much to it when it will serve a turn. Of the acceptance he says Jacob agreed without insisting on submission or restitution, peace and love being jewels so valuable that we can scarcely buy them too dearly, and better to sit down losers than go on in strife. He sets out both the terms and the forms. Jacob was bound to be a good husband, neither afflicting his wives nor marrying others — an engagement he had given no cause to require, and required by the man who afflicted them himself, for the injurious are commonly the most jealous of others. The forms were the pillar and the heap, raised to keep the memory when agreements were not put in writing; a sacrifice of peace-offerings, our peace with God being what puts true comfort into our peace with friends; the eating of bread together, by which such covenants were anciently ratified; and the appeal to God as witness and judge.

Clarke observes that Jegar-sahadutha is pure Chaldee and Galeed pure Hebrew with the same sense, and infers that Chaldee was nearly coeval with Hebrew; he notes that the word rendered heap means properly a round heap, made probably to serve as altar and table both. Wesley observes which name lasted — Galeed, Jacob's, not Laban's.

Keil says Jacob's words cut Laban to the heart, so that he turned, offered his hand and proposed a covenant. Ellicott hears it otherwise, as an affectionate answer that ignores the invectives: why should Laban wish to injure Jacob, when all that Jacob had was still his in the best of senses, the wives being his daughters and the children his grandsons? On the languages he holds Aramaic to have been the ordinary speech of Mesopotamia, but thinks Laban's family spoke Hebrew too, since he names the place Mizpah with a Hebrew word and his daughters gave their sons Hebrew names.

48.pericope_label: Mizpah, the terms of the oath, and the God invoked as judge

schools.summary: Gill takes the heap for a witness of the covenant and against them if they broke it, and observes that Mizpah, being Hebrew, might seem Jacob's naming, though what follows shows it Laban's. He reads the clause about the wives broadly, of affliction in body or mind, by blows or ill words or withholding food and raiment; and on the God invoked he holds the father meant to be Terah, so the god of Abraham and Nahor here is not the true God, or not as truly worshipped, but what Terah and Nahor served while idolaters and Laban served still, though less grossly. Calvin fastens on what the name commits them to: Laban refers to God's judgment whatever either may do against the other out of sight — though the knowledge never reach me, the Lord, who is everywhere, will see it. If natural feeling taught even Laban that frauds hidden from men come before God, those who have the gospel should be ashamed to seek a covert for their own; and here is the legitimate use of an oath, that men end their controversies by resorting to God's judgment. On the wives he points at the irony: Laban calls it perfidy for Jacob to take another wife, when it was Laban who forced him into polygamy, the holy man having more wives than one only because Leah was craftily substituted for Rachel — and when the bond of marriage is broken, than which nothing among men is more sacred, the whole of human society sinks into decay.

Clarke thinks the verses badly divided and would read the naming together. Mizpah means a watch-tower, and Laban's thought is that God, the place being consecrated, would take possession of the heap and stand on it, keeping either party from trenching on the terms. He observes that although all were present at the sacrifice, the contract was made by the two men apart, with God alone called to witness, and explains the fear behind it — Jacob had four wives already, and Laban dreaded others whose children would share the inheritance to the prejudice of his daughters and grandchildren. He catches a textual difficulty too: Laban speaks of the pillar as cast by himself when the narrative said Jacob set it up, and credits one Hebrew and one Samaritan manuscript with the true reading, thou hast set up. On the judge invoked he argues that Laban certainly speaks of the true God, and meets the objection about Terah's idolatry by preferring the reading your father, which several manuscripts support and which is the form Laban used earlier when addressing Jacob alone.

Ellicott sees a play on the pillar, whose Hebrew name is close in sound, and draws more from the sentence attached: Laban there calls Jacob's God Jehovah, a name he can only have learned from Jacob, which proves not merely some Hebrew but that the two had talked together about religion, and that he was no mere idolater for all his calling the teraphim his gods. On the judge he settles the matter from the grammar: the verb is plural, be they judges, which suggests that Laban took Abraham's Elohim for one being and Nahor's for another, so we ought to render the gods of their father — as though Abraham had taken one of Terah's gods and Nahor another, which is polytheism of the ancient kind that made gods local beings with powers bounded by a district. Against all of it he sets Jacob's oath, sworn by the one Being who was the sole object of his father's worship.

54.pericope_label: The sacrifice on the mount, and Laban's departure

schools.summary: Gill denies it was worship: Jacob slew cattle for a feast, as Jarchi explains the phrase, such feasts being usual between parties in covenant, and in a religious act he could neither have joined with Laban nor admitted him. Of the parting he has Laban rise early, kiss the sons who were his grandsons and the daughters Rachel and Leah with Dinah, as relations parted in those countries, wish them happiness, and return to Haran, after which we hear no more of him — neither when nor where he died, his name occurring once again in Jacob's mouth. Calvin reads the whole close as evidence of a guardian: Jacob showed his kindness in entertaining as guests the kinsmen who had ill-used him, and Moses means us to see that it was by God's special favour that so placid a serenity shone out after a storm which had threatened the holy man with destruction. The friendly parting he assigns to the same cause, the Lord manifesting himself as his servant's keeper by delivering him, like a lost sheep, out of the jaws of the wolf — for not only was Laban's fury appeased, but he put on a paternal affection, as though he had been changed into another man. On the blessing he fastens on the person rather than the act: Laban had lapsed from true piety and his manners were unholy, yet the habit of blessing stayed with him, which teaches that some principles of divine knowledge remain in the hearts of the wicked, leaving them no excuse of ignorance; for the custom of blessing arises from men's being persuaded that God alone is the author of every good thing.

Clarke thinks it likely that Laban did join in the solemn rite, and that having offered the blood and the fat to God the company feasted upon the sacrifice. He counts the party at the parting as the eleven sons with Dinah and their mothers, all of whom Laban had claimed as his own, and marks what the blessing cost: he prayed heartily for their prosperity though he had come bound by a vow to do them injury, so that God turned his intended curse into a blessing. He closes with two verdicts and a difficulty. Of Jacob he says that hitherto there has been little in his character to admire, but that a blessed change in both mind and conduct is soon to appear. Of Laban he judges more carefully than the others: he does not seem to have been what we commonly call a wicked man, but he was weak and covetous, and covetousness extinguished in him, as in all its votaries, the principles of righteousness and benevolence and the very charities of human life — so that provided his own store increased he cared not who was wronged, and let his own children want necessaries. The difficulty is chronological: Jacob's age at going to Laban had been fixed almost universally at seventy-seven, but Clarke reports Kennicott, following Skinner, as holding that it cannot stand, since Jacob was a hundred and thirty at his going down into Egypt and Joseph, then ten years governor, had been made governor at thirty, so Jacob can have been no more than ninety when Joseph was born; on the received reckoning Judah begets Er at thirteen, Er marries at nine, Onan at eight, and the eleven sons and Dinah are all crowded into five years.

Ellicott shows why the question is hard: the sense is that Jacob slaughtered cattle and made a feast, but since animals were at first killed only for sacrifice and flesh eaten on no other occasion, Hebrew cannot distinguish the two acts.
